input.question: How much of the "snow" on an analog T.V. is from the cosmic microwave background radiation?
input.ground_truth: > but I have no idea to estimate how many pixels are actually being lit up by CMBR. Zero. And very little of the overall noise is due to CMBR Thermal noise is a much much larger contributor than CMBR (by a factor of between 100 and 1,000) to the 'snowy' picture on analog televisions. In [this](_URL_0_) thread /u/MrDerpleton provides some great information on how the 'snow' pattern becomes rendered.

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: How much of the "snow" on an analog T.V. is from the cosmic microwave background radiation?

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have an old TV with "snow" on the screen when there’s no channel. That "snow" is like tiny dots and lines that move around.

Now, the whole universe is full of very, very tiny invisible waves called "microwave radiation." Some of these waves come from the very beginning of the universe, and scientists call them the "cosmic microwave background." But these waves are super, super weak—like a whisper you can barely hear.

When you see "snow" on your old TV, it’s mostly because the TV isn’t picking up any real TV signal, so it shows random stuff. Most of that "snow" is actually just the TV’s own noise and the weak signals from things around you, like radios or even the wires in your house.

The cosmic microwave background is there, all around us, but it’s so weak that the TV can’t pick it up at all. So, almost none of the "snow" on your TV comes from the cosmic microwave background. It’s mostly just the TV being confused and showing random patterns.

So, if you think of the "snow" as a big bowl of mixed-up puzzle pieces, the cosmic microwave background is just one teeny, tiny piece that you can’t even see in there!
